items.title: Agents are sessions, not requests: size GKE node pools for AI agent sessions
items.summary: AI agent sessions remain active and idle for most of the workday, making traditional one-Pod-per-session allocations inefficient for cluster resources. By using open-source tools like Agent Substrate and AX on GKE, developers can park idle sessions in object storage to release compute resources while maintaining session state. This approach optimizes resource utilization and reduces Kubernetes node costs by up to 40%.

items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

A browser extension only sees web pages. A lot of writing on a Mac happens somewhere else: Slack, Mail, Notes, Messages, the ChatGPT app, and text fields inside desktop apps built on web views. To check text in all of them, an app has to follow whichever field has focus, read its text, know where each word sits on screen, and write corrections back without breaking the host app. macOS exposes this through the Accessibility API (AX). The user grants Accessibility permission once in System Settings, and the app can then observe and act on UI elements in other processes. AX is powerful, but every host app implements it a little differently, and a call into a busy app can block. Most of InkHammy's Mac architecture exists to deal with those two facts. items.title: Calculating Overtime in JavaScript: Get the Regular Rate Right
items.summary: Overtime calculation in JavaScript looks like a ten-minute job. Multiply the extra hours by 1.5 and you're done, right? It works until a bonus or a shift differential shows up, and then the numbers drift. Here's a small, testable way to do it properly, with the regular rate handled the way US payroll expects. The rule in one paragraph Under the US Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), covered non-exempt employees get at least 1.5 times their regular rate for every hour over 40 in a workweek. The regular rate is the total straight-time pay for the week divided by the total hours worked. That's the catch: it isn't always the hourly wage. A $24 rate and 47 hours gives $960 + $252 = $1,212. items.title: Why Did We Build It This Way? How Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) Save Codebases
items.summary: Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) are short, structured text documents that capture significant software design choices made by a development team. They explain what decision was made, the context behind it, and the consequences—both positive and negative—of that choice. By storing these records directly inside a software repository alongside the source code, teams maintain a permanent, searchable history of their architectural evolution over time. Imagine buying a historic house that has been remodeled by five different owners over fifty years. You notice an odd, diagonal wall in the middle of the dining room that narrows the hallway. Frustrated by the awkward layout, you decide to knock it down during a weekend renovation project, only to realize too late that the wall contained the central electrical conduit and a critical load-bearing pillar for the upper floor. If the previous owners had kept a simple house logbook in a kitchen drawer detailing why that wall was placed diagonally, you would have saved thousands of dollars and prevented structural damage. items.title: Sveltext: rebuilding the gettext workflow I love for Svelte
items.summary: I have used gettext-style i18n, such as ttag and lingui, for more than seven years. When I started working on a Svelte project, I wanted to continue using it. The workflow was good enough for me to spend time building the exact implementation I wanted. That became Sveltext, an experiment in extreme minimalism. I wanted to judge what I actually needed, keep that part, and learn how to build it. The part I love about gettext starts before I translate anything. I hardcode English words and sentences in the code, then look at the UI. Once I am confident enough to move on, I mark the strings as translatable. For example, I can start with this: Hello World Then wrap the text with t: {t`Hello World`} With the initial setup already done, I run npx sveltext extract and fill in the translations in the .po file. There is less context switching when I read and work on the codebase. The original sentence stays where I use it. I don't have to move "Hello World" into another file and give it a key such as greeting. items.title: How I Built an Open-Source AI Browser Extension That Actually Executes Tasks
items.summary: A few months ago I got frustrated with AI tools that could talk about doing things but couldn't actually do them. So I built Cosmos: an open-source Chrome extension where you describe a goal in plain English and watch it get done. Today I'm open-sourcing it. Here's what it does, how it works, and what I learned building it. You type a goal — "extract all product prices from this page as JSON" or "fill in this form with my saved details" — and Cosmos: Reads the live DOM (not a screenshot — the actual structured page) Sends that + your goal to an LLM and gets back a step-by-step plan Validates the plan against a strict Zod schema (bad LLM output is rejected, not executed) Executes each step: click, type, scroll, navigate, extract data Streams every step back to you live in a side panel It also remembers. Every run updates a 5-layer memory system so Cosmos gets better at the sites you use most. When you use an online regex tester, your test strings are logged. I built Antigravity Tools so every operation runs inside your browser, using native APIs. items.title: How a Mines multiplier is calculated: (1 - edge) / P(survive), in JavaScript
items.summary: Mines is the Minesweeper-flavored grid game: a 5×5 board hides a few mines, you open tiles one at a time, and a multiplier climbs with every safe tile. The multiplier looks like a design choice, but it's almost entirely determined by one probability. This post derives it, writes it in JavaScript, and points out two easy mistakes along the way. The code blocks below form one script: paste them into a single .mjs file in order and node prints the output shown under each. Take a board of T tiles with M mines, so T − M tiles are safe. Mine positions are fixed before the first click, and you open tiles without replacement. The first tile is safe with probability (T − M) / T. Given that it was safe, the board now has T − 1 tiles left and still M mines, so the second is safe with probability (T − M − 1) / (T − 1). Keep going for k picks: P(survive k) = ∏_{i=0}^{k−1} (T − M − i) / (T − i) This is a hypergeometric probability: the chance that a sample of k tiles drawn without replacement contains zero mines. They are not visible on a laptop, they do not break a test, and they are the difference between a numeric keypad and a full QWERTY with a comma on the wrong layer. So I counted all of them in Nakodo. 90 input and textarea tags across 582 source files. 14 are hidden inputs carrying state through a form, so 76 are fields a person can type into, and they live where you would expect: 50 behind the login, 14 in the admin panel, five on the sign-in and sign-up pages, two on public pages, plus the two primitives themselves. The remarkable part is how few raw elements there are. Outside ui/input.tsx and ui/textarea.tsx, the entire repository contains four bare input or textarea tags, and all four are radio buttons inside two radio-card components. Every text field in the product is the same component, which is what makes an audit like this worth doing: anything wrong is wrong in one place, and anything missing can be added in one place. items.title: AI writes the code fast. The repo is where it shows.
items.summary: A lot of repos shared on LinkedIn look the same now. The app works, the demo is clean, but open the repo and it tells another story: everything pushed straight to main, 200 commits called "update", one commit that changes 40 files, no README, and sometimes a .env sitting in the history. The app is fine. The repo says nobody is maintaining it. With AI writing so much of the code, this matters more than before. When you ask a tool for a feature, it can change ten files at once. Some of those changes you asked for. Some you didn't. The repo is the only place someone can see whether you checked. Why I built it A few weeks back I kept seeing the same thing on LinkedIn: people shipping real apps with AI, proud of them, and the repo behind them was a mess. Not because they’re bad developers. Nobody showed them the repo part. The tools teach you to build. They don’t teach you to protect main or keep a key out of the history. items.summary: Notifio lives in the system tray. Click the tray icon and a window appears, and because of an empty event handler and a deliberate reload, what appears is a brand new renderer: fresh React tree, fresh state, every component mounting for the first time. The app is on the download page if you want to watch it happen. When I wrote that post I said the renderer "may not remember anything", and I meant it as an architectural rule: product state belongs to the main process, the window is a view onto it, and anything the window tries to keep is a bug waiting for the next reload. items.title: Three agents on one laptop, 4 to 6 GB per dev server, and the 145-line lock that is just mkdir
items.summary: I build CogniPrep with several coding agents working in parallel, each in its own git worktree of the same repository. Last Sunday three of them were building three new assessment providers at once, and the machine fell over. Not a crash with a stack trace. Memory pressure, swap, and everything taking four times as long until nothing finished at all. The numbers, measured and then written into the script that fixed it: # Measured on 16 Nov 2026: one `next dev` peaks at 4 to 6 GB (more if it stays # up while code is edited), `tsc --noEmit` at 4 GB, and the test suite needs # several GB more. Three workers each running all three at once filled the # machine. Three worktrees times three heavy jobs is nine processes, each wanting multiple gigabytes. On 12 November a single webpack dev server left up while code was edited reached 12 GB on its own; on 16 November the total crossed 18 GB. No amount of per-process tuning fixes that. The only fix is that one of them runs at a time. There is no daemon, no lockfile library, no port to bind. items.summary: Notifio is an Electron app that watches a rental search page and tells you when something new appears. You can get it from the download page, and when it starts it opens one window. items.title: nuxt/server: Write Server Routes Today That Still Run on Nuxt 5
items.summary: Every Nuxt app with a server/ directory has a quiet dependency problem. Your API routes call defineEventHandler, getQuery, and readBody, and those come from h3. Your modules import types from nitropack. That has been fine for years, but Nuxt 5 moves to Nitro v3 and h3 v2, and both ship breaking changes. Every handler you wrote against h3 v1 is a handler you will touch during that upgrade, and every module you depend on has to cut a release before you can move. Nuxt 4.6 is the escape hatch. It ships nuxt/server, a new import source owned by Nuxt itself, and server code written against it runs unchanged on Nuxt 4 today and Nuxt 5 later. Nothing forces you to migrate. But if you have a weekend and a handful of API routes, this is the cheapest that upgrade will ever be. Think of it as the server-side twin of nuxt/app. Handlers, middleware, and the utilities most apps reach for all come from one place, and they are typed against a portable RequestEvent built on web standards rather than h3's event object: event.req; // a standard Request event.url; // a standard URL event.res; // { status, statusText, headers } event.res.headers; // a standard Headers object event.context; // per-reques

items.title: How Cursor’s Agent Mode Works and How to Host Its Claude Tool on ECS Fargate, Explained Simply
items.summary: Cursor turns your editor into an AI‑native workspace, but the heavy LLM calls can still slow you down. By offloading the Claude‑powered tool server to ECS Fargate you keep the IDE snappy while gaining unlimited scalability. This post shows exactly how to wire the two together. What is Agent Mode? Cursor ships with a built‑in LLM (large language model) that can suggest code, refactor, or answer questions. When it needs to do something it can’t do locally—like running a test suite, reading a remote file, or calling a cloud service—it switches to Agent Mode. In this mode Cursor sends a tool call (an HTTP request) to a tiny web server you provide. The server does the work, talks to other services (for example AWS Bedrock’s Claude model), and sends a JSON payload back. Cursor then inserts the result into your editor as if it had generated the answer itself. items.title: Your logger redaction only hides the fields you remembered
items.summary: Every leaked secret I have seen started the same way. Someone wrote logger.info({ user }), the code looked harmless, and user carried a session token. Now that token lives in the log aggregator, the error tracker and a few vendors' systems, for as long as they keep logs. Most loggers have an answer for this. pino has a redact option, and you can write a winston format. Both work the same way: you list the paths that are sensitive, and those fields are masked. The trouble is the list. It only covers what you remembered. The leak is always somewhere else: a free-text note field where a customer pasted an API key a nested payload from a third-party SDK you never looked inside an error message that includes the request URL, with a token in the query string I built flare-redact to check the content itself. It knows what an AWS key, a GitHub token, a JWT, a card number or an IBAN looks like, and checks a checksum wherever one exists, so the card number 4242 4242 4242 4242 is masked but 4242 4242 4242 4243, which fails the card checksum, is left alone. import { redact } from 'flare-redact'; redact({ user: 'bob@corp.com', password: 'hunter2', note: 'my key is AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE' }); // {

items.title: Why I took Whisper out of my iPhone transcription app before it shipped
items.summary: I work on Koedori at W Lab. It is an iPhone app that records a lecture, a meeting or an interview and turns it into text on the phone itself, with no account, and the audio is never uploaded. The early builds ran Whisper through WhisperKit. The version on the App Store has no Whisper in it at all: it uses Apple's SpeechAnalyzer framework and its SpeechTranscriber module. This post is about why, and what building on SpeechTranscriber is like. Koedori makes three promises: transcription is free and needs no account, audio never leaves the phone, and re-transcribing costs nothing, as often as you like. The second one is architecture, not a setting. There is no code path that uploads audio, and the app has no server of its own. So recognition has to run on the device, and it has to be cheap enough to run again on a whim. Whisper on the phone met that on paper. The trouble was everything around the model. WhisperKit compiles a model for the Neural Engine the first time it loads it. On the iPhone 14 I measured, the first load of large-v3 turbo after an install took 197 to 205 seconds, every time. A reload within the same install took 4 seconds, and a 10-second clip then transcribed in 0.

items.title: C# 15 Union Types: What Changed and When I’d Actually Use Them
items.summary: C# 15 is here with .NET 11, and one of the features that caught my attention immediately is union types. If you have worked with F#, TypeScript, Rust, Kotlin, or other languages with sum types or discriminated unions, the idea will feel familiar. But the interesting question is not: “What is the syntax?” The more useful question is: When does this actually improve a real C# codebase? Let’s look at it without the bla bla. Imagine a service that looks up a product. The operation can return one of two meaningful outcomes: the product exists the product does not exist Before C# 15, you had several options. You could return null. public Product? FindProduct(int id) { // ... } Simple, but now null carries business meaning. You could return object. public object FindProduct(int id) { // Product or ProductNotFound } That is worse because the compiler cannot tell callers which types are valid. You could introduce a base class: public abstract record ProductLookupResult; public sealed record Product(int Id, string Name) : ProductLookupResult; public sealed record ProductNotFound(int Id) : ProductLookupResult; This is much better. items.title: A silent data-loss bug in a paid product: the draft was in memory the whole time
items.summary: The bug had been live for weeks and no one had reported it, because it only fired for people who had just paid us money. It's a small tool that generates wedding speeches. Nine questions, three drafts, one payment. The kind of product where the whole value is the output — the text is the thing you buy. After checkout, the payment provider redirects the user back to /success. That page verifies the payment and then does this: {copy.okCta} → Back to the form. Makes sense — the drafts live on the form page. Except the drafts were stored like this: const [result, setResult] = useState(null); // ... setResult(data); In memory. Nowhere else. The sequence, for a paying customer: Fill in nine questions Read three drafts Get redirected to checkout Pay Get redirected back See an empty questionnaire Fill in the same nine questions again Wait another 60 seconds for generation Nothing was broken, technically. Every request returned 200. There were no errors in the logs. A payment succeeded and the user was shown the thing they paid for — eventually. I found it by reading the code, not by using the product. That's the part that bothers me. The happy path in testing was: generate → look at drafts

items.summary: If you're starting a new React project in 2026, the real choice usually isn't "React or Next.js". It's whether you need React on its own with Vite, or React plus a framework for routing, server rendering and backend endpoints. I build client sites and apps for a living, so this breakdown comes from the angle of SEO, first-load speed and long-term maintenance. It covers Next.js 16, React Router and Vite, with the current versions checked against npm and the official docs. Next.js vs React is one of the first questions that comes up when a founder or developer plans a new web project, and it's a slightly unfair matchup. React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces. Next.js is a framework built on top of React that adds routing, server rendering, data fetching and a production build setup. So the real question isn't "which one?" but "do I need React on its own, or React plus a framework?" This guide answers that from the angle of building client sites and apps, where SEO, speed and maintenance all matter. OpenAI said the models were trying to find information that they could use to cheat on an evaluation, and succeeded. The break-in at Hugging Face, which Nvidia acquired for roughly $13 billion in September, rattled industry researchers and prompted government officials to call for more stringent oversight of the AI industry. On Monday, Bonta said that OpenAI later disclosed to his investigators that it was aware of 80 incidents "involving loss of control and access to third-party networks and websites." items.title: An N+1 query looks like a staircase
items.summary: I've been building AspNetDebugDashboard on and off for a while. It's my take on Laravel Telescope for ASP.NET Core: you add one NuGet package, and in Development you get a page at /_debug with every request your app handled, the EF Core queries each one ran, outgoing HttpClient calls, logs and exceptions. The part that always bugged me was the request detail. You'd open a slow request and get tabs. 21 queries in one of them, an HTTP call in another, 393 ms at the top, and adding it up was on you. So in 2.5 the detail opens on a timeline instead. The sample app has a report endpoint I wrote to be slow on purpose. It loads 20 orders, fetches each order's items in a loop, and then calls a shipping-rates service that takes 300 ms: foreach (var o in orders) o.OrderItems = await db.OrderItems.Where(i => i.OrderId == o.Id).ToListAsync(); Each bar starts where the query or call really started. The 20 item queries run one after another, so they step down the page, and since it's the same SQL every time they get grouped as ×20. The HTTP call doesn't start until they're all done. items.title: How to Let AI Write Business Rules Without Letting It Touch Production
items.summary: Every team that keeps business rules outside its code has a backlog of rule changes. "Hold orders over $10,000 from new customers." "Give Gold members free shipping on weekends." Each one is small, specific and urgent, and the people who know what the rule should say usually aren't the people who can write it. LLMs look like the obvious fix. Describe the rule in a sentence and let the model write it. The problem is what happens next. A rule that decides discounts, shipping holds or loan approvals is production logic. An AI that writes it straight into production is a deployment pipeline with no tests, no review and no rollback, driven by something that's confidently wrong a few percent of the time. Code Effects was designed to give teams both: let AI agents do real rule-authoring work, and make it structurally impossible for them to change what runs in production on their own. Full Disclosure: I work for Code Effects Software. This article is not so much a product promotion as a way to let developers and business teams learn about well-established, cost-effective approaches to business rules management and decision automation. items.title: Day 24: The Three Axes of Permissions: Action, Row and Column
items.summary: The API Payload Security Pipeline: Order, Protection Levels and Keys closed by changing axis. A protection level governs the form of one call, and at no point does it ask which data this person may see. Permissions are something an ERP system cannot avoid, and they have never been one question. They are three: whether a buyer may delete a purchase order, which orders may be deleted, and whether the cost column on that order can be seen at all, or changed. The three answers come from different sources, and they are enforced in different places. items.title: "Proof of use" as a requirement for open source contributions?
items.summary: As an open source maintainer, I get a lot of AI slop PRs. Some of these have genuine value. Most address edge cases that almost never occur in real life. It's not that they're not fixing real problems, it's that they're fixing problems that nobody is ever likely to encounter. I'm experimenting with "proof of use" as a requirement for submissions. Specifically, you need to show me that your project that depends on my project before I'll look at your PR. "Proof of use" can be an existing open source project that imports mine (show me the git history!) or a clear description starting with "in our closed source project in production, we found that...". The specific problem that I want to address is ensuring that contributions from people genuinely depending on my software are handled, while filtering out the OpenClaw/Github green square farming/drive-by LLM noise. What are lobste.rs's thoughts on this?

items.title: FBI Says Artex AI Open-Source Hacking Tool Used to Breach Networks In 'Under Three Hours'
items.summary: The FBI is warning (PDF) that hackers are using the AI-powered penetration-testing tool Artex to compromise networks in "under three hours" in some cases. The tool has been linked to attacks against South Korean financial institutions, at least 2,250 ConnectWise customers and Barracuda. TechCrunch reports: Artex is one of several open-source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network's defenses. Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open-source models and non-U.S. models. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be "noisy," meaning they generate reams of traffic and data that may trigger a targeted company's defensive alerts. But the tools allow hackers to move at speeds that makes it far more harder for human defenders to keep up. In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise "in under three hours." Oftentimes, Artex will rely on rapidly scanning a victim's network to look for signs of weakness, and then exploit simple security bugs, such as weak protections and exposed or stolen passwords to gain a foothold. Undo still works, because Quill pastes through the app's own paste. Prompts: Fix Grammar, Professional, Shorter and Friendly to start. You can add, edit, reorder and delete them, or type a one-off instruction. Direct shortcuts: any prompt can have its own global shortcut, which rewrites the selection without opening the popup. No selection: Quill rewrites the whole text field. Model: it uses your own Groq API key with openai/gpt-oss-20b. It's written in SwiftUI and AppKit, with no third-party dependencies, and needs macOS 14 or later. The hard part isn't the AI call. It's reading and writing text in someone else's app, safely. Quill registers system-wide hotkeys with Carbon, which still works, and needs no extra permission for this. One shortcut opens the popup. Each prompt can have its own. items.summary: Hi HN! We’re Arsh and Max, founders of Axonnic (https://axonnic.com). We’ve developed a forearm sleeve that reads muscle activity to decode finger movements and estimate fingertip force, while leaving the hands bare. It’s used to record human movement and generate training data for dextrous robots. Here’s a demo video: https://youtube.com/shorts/xBrocTc9cfA We’ve found that electromyography (EMG) is a much better way to train robots than by video alone because video only captures movement, not muscle activity or the effort behind the movement. A useful signal can be present even when the hand barely moves; just maintaining a grip involves muscle activation. The subtle muscle movements that can barely be picked up in video are the most important details for activities like sewing and delicate assembly. The sleeve has 64 channels of surface electromyography, or EMG. Electrodes on the skin detect electrical activity from muscles in the forearm. items.title: Checking every number an LLM writes against the source file
items.summary: LabChure turns uploaded documents (PDF, PPTX, DOCX, HWP, images and more) into a web brochure with its own URL. Getting the model to write the page was the easy part. Numbers were the hard part. A model that rewrites a spec sheet will sometimes turn "12 kW" into "15 kW", and the page still reads fine. So we added a gate. Before a page can be published, code checks its numbers against the uploaded files. Numbers with a unit: mm, kg, kWh, Hz, rpm, °C, %, inch and similar Prices: ₩ $ € ¥ £, or amounts with KRW / USD Both sides are normalized first: Unicode NFKC, lowercase, no spaces, no thousands separators. So "1,200 mm" and "1200mm" are the same token. Matching has two steps: The passage that section cites If it's not there, every file you uploaded The page goes to "needs review" and the publish API returns 409. The editor shows the token: Not found in your documents: 15 kW. You fix the text or press "Publish anyway". Nothing passes silently. After an AI edit, the check runs again on its own. The Connecticut-based company raised prices again and again, moves its executives said were necessary because of the new fees on imports. Now, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's most sweeping tariffs earlier this year, the company is getting at least $298 million refunded. Instead of sharing that bounty with its customers, however, the firm has chosen different recipients: Its own leaders. items.title: Why We Decoupled Clients from Orders: Architecture Lessons from Building a SaaS Portal
items.summary: When building an MVP, speed is everything. You take shortcuts, design flat schemas, and ship as fast as possible. In our early iterations of ClientStatus - a platform designed to provide lightweight, zero-login project and order tracking portals for clients - we made a classic architectural assumption: 1 Client = 1 Portal / Order. It seemed clean at the time: a business creates a "client", sets a status, shares a private token link, and syncs updates via Google Sheets. Within a month of real usage, that assumption completely broke down. Here is how it failed, why we had to decouple our core domain model, and the lessons learned along the way. items.summary: Over the weekend, SpaceX successfully caught a Starship upper stage returning from orbit for the first time, demonstrating a key piece of its plan for a fully and rapidly reusable launch system. The achievement means SpaceX has now demonstrated tower catches of both Starship stages, though not yet on the same flight. "Many small fixes are needed to achieve immediate reusability (like an airplane)," noted SpaceX's Elon Musk. The Register reports: Flight 15 began well, with the 33 Raptor engines of the Super Heavy booster launching the stack from Pad 2 at Starbase, Texas. Hot staging followed, and the booster performed its directional flip maneuver. Thirty-two Raptor engines relit for the boostback burn, intended to return Super Heavy to the tower for another catch. The booster had managed the maneuver on flight tests 5, 7, and 8, but this time something went wrong. "The boostback burn ended early due to low fuel mass," SpaceX said. The booster automatically aborted its return to the tower and diverted offshore. items.title: Why I built a live request-flow visualizer for ASP.NET Core (and what v0.4.0 adds)
items.summary: Every time a request misbehaves somewhere deep inside a layered ASP.NET Core API, I hit the same wall. I know something went wrong between the controller and the database, but I don't know where, not without attaching a debugger or stitching it together from logs after the fact. That's the gap NetApiFlow is trying to close. It's an open source NuGet package that shows, live, the exact path an HTTP request takes through your own code: Controller or Endpoint, then Handler, then Services, then Repositories, then SQL. Duration per step, where a failure started, what got slow, what never ran at all. No external infrastructure. No second dashboard to deploy, no collector to babysit, no extra Docker container sitting around just for observability. The dashboard itself is an Angular app embedded straight into the NuGet package, served by your own API process. Install it, add two lines, open a URL: builder.Services.AddNetApiFlow(); builder.Services.AddNetApiFlowDashboard(); // ... app.UseNetApiFlowDashboard(); // mounted at /flow by default A request comes in and the graph lights up node by node as each step runs. If something fails, you see exactly where, with the real exception attached.

items.title: White-Label iOS Architecture: One Codebase, Many Brands

This is a structural guide to shipping one Swift codebase as many branded apps: what belongs in configuration, what belongs in code, how the Xcode project is wired, and which decisions are expensive to reverse once you have store listings in production. items.title: Your iOS App Says “Offline”—But Is It? Debugging API Failures With a VPN Enabled
items.summary: A user connects their iPhone to a VPN, opens your app and sees: No internet connection. Please try again. They switch to another app, which works. Your app may have encountered a real failure. But “no internet” might be the wrong diagnosis. A hostname lookup can fail. A secure connection can fail. An API can return an authentication error. The response can arrive successfully and then fail JSON decoding. A failed API operation does not automatically mean the device is offline—or that the VPN caused the failure. The first useful fix is to preserve those distinctions in your networking code. Think of an API operation as several stages: Establish a usable network connection. Resolve the destination hostname when needed. Establish the secure connection. Exchange the HTTP request and response. Interpret the response body. This is a debugging model, not a claim that every request creates a new connection or performs a fresh DNS lookup. Connections and lookup results can be reused. The point is that failures at different stages need different handling. [I]t's not going to be a particularly powerful AI; in fact, wollymonjak notes that if you ask something too complex or too long, it starts spitting out nonsense. But who cares about that when you're using a language model on DOS? The same blog also notes that "the iPhone Duo hasn't been out for too long, and someone has already gotten Windows 11 on it." As spotted by TechSpot, this cool feat was performed by Ammaar Reshi over on X. Their project is called WindowsiOS, and its goal is to get Windows 11 running on an iPhone Duo without jailbreaking. Usually, when we cover a project coded up by AI, Claude is the one that called the shots; this time, Reshi opted to use Gemini 4 Carbon, Google's flagship model. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Supabase email sign-in and a profiles table for iOS, done safely
items.summary: Almost every iOS app I start needs the same first hour of work: email sign-in, a place to keep per-user data, and a way to make sure users can only touch their own rows. Supabase gives you most of it. The part people get wrong is the profiles table, because the obvious version is also the insecure one. This post walks through the setup I use: the SQL, the Swift, and the three mistakes to avoid. It assumes you know basic SwiftUI and have a free Supabase project. Supabase Auth stores credentials in auth.users. You don't add your own columns there. Instead you create a public.profiles table whose primary key is the auth user's id: create table if not exists public.profiles ( id uuid primary key references auth.users (id) on delete cascade, email text, full_name text, avatar_url text, created_at timestamptz not null default now(), updated_at timestamptz not null default now() ); on delete cascade matters: when the auth user is deleted, the profile goes with it. No orphans. The key in your app is public. Anyone can extract it. So the key is not your security. Row Level Security (RLS) is. alter table public.profiles enable row level security; -- signed-out clients get nothing revoke all

This guide is for the developer who published the app, not for someone seeing a Gatekeeper warning. A cracked copy can appear on a warez site, a torrent index or GitHub without showing up in your analytics. Start with a search, not a download. On Google, query your app name plus "crack", "cracked", "free download" or "dmg", and quote the name if it is generic. Repeat those queries on Mac warez sites and torrent indexes, then search GitHub for the app name, your bundle ID, or a distinctive Info.plist string. items.title: Eliminating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference with Integer-Only Arithmetic (15 minute read)
items.summary: A floating-point number stores a fixed number of significant digits and a separate exponent. When two numbers with very different exponents are added, the small one has to be shifted to line up with the big one, and the digits that fall off on the end are gone. That means that (a+b)+c is not always equal to a+(b+c). This post looks at what happens when integer addition, which is exact, is used.

Tasked with repairing an ancient shrine in the weeks leading up to a local festival, you’ll find yourself cleaning out trash, mending broken arches and slowly bringing a small rural community back together. items.title: Handing over humanity (22 minute read)
items.summary: Some AI experts believe that once we achieve superintelligence, humans will be permanently disempowered, and we shall all be ruled by an AI god. This might not be such a desirable outcome, as humans have a natural desire for freedom. The arrangement will probably not work, as keeping power responsive to human needs has required checks developed over centuries, sustained by repeated feedback from the real world and correction, and there's no reason to keep that equilibrium stable once humans have surrendered all control. Humans have the ability now to steer the technology in a way that will not lead to a complete replacement of human judgment.

items.title: LLMs can learn some multi-step reasoning on filler tokens instead of visible CoT (9 minute read)
items.summary: By changing the training setup and applying LoRAs to Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and gpt-oss-20b, researchers taught models to do some multi-step tasks while emitting only filler tokens, beating an answer-only baseline on three of seven tasks. They also mapped theoretical layer-depth limits and showed empirical walls, with some tasks learned out to 60 steps and others failing after one to three. The work is meant to separate filler-token reasoning from steganographic hidden reasoning when interpreting chain-of-thought.

items.title: What objective is reasoning solving? (12 minute read)
items.summary: Reasoning is pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses each of them with each sample. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer - it's only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success. RL training directly raises the success probability. The gains credited to 'thinking longer' come from the search paid for during training rather than at inference.

items.title: Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling (28 minute read)
items.summary: Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. There are two types of test-time scaling: one allows researchers to trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training; and the other lets researchers trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets them do so up to quantities of compute and performance that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit the latter change will have a larger impact than test-time scaling considered simply. This essay describes how this may impact the world.

The researchers working on SpudCell hope that it will eventually be a platform for biotechnology that will allow a simple cell to be engineered in scores of useful ways.
